Between 1790 and 1860, roughly a million enslaved people were sold from the Upper South to the Deep South.

Not captured abroad. Bought and moved internally, by Americans, inside the United States.

a thread 🧵🗺️

1/ Compare the panels. In 1790 slavery is coastal: the Chesapeake tidewater and the rice country of South Carolina and Georgia. By 1860 the darkest colour has swung southwest, into Alabama, Mississippi, Louisiana and east Texas.

2/ Two things drove that. The cotton gin, patented in 1794, made short-staple cotton profitable across the southern interior. Then in 1808 the US banned the international slave trade — closing the Atlantic supply just as demand exploded inland.

3/ So the trade turned inward. Virginia, Maryland and Kentucky became exporters of people to the new cotton states. Firms advertised in newspapers and kept holding pens in Alexandria, Richmond and Natchez. Historians call it the Second Middle Passage.

4/ It was mostly sale, not migration. Families were separated at the point of transaction, and the journey south was often made on foot in chained coffles. Roughly a million people, over about seventy years.

5/ Where they ended up wasn't random. The darkest band follows the Black Belt — a crescent of heavy prairie soil weathered from Cretaceous chalk, laid down when the Gulf reached far further north. Excellent cotton ground.

6/ Which means a geological formation from ~100 million years ago is visible on an 1860 census map. It shows up again later in maps of Black population share and of voting patterns. The soil is still there; so are the consequences.

This week's Lines & Legends goes into the 1861 map of this data that Lincoln kept in his office — and what he was reading in the pale areas. Free, every 3 days: https://buttondown.com/forummapping
